hints: Look at the y-axis first. Atrial pressure is very low (only about 0 to 2 kPa) compared to ventricular and aortic pressure, so focus on the lowest dotted curve.
Atrial systole is a small squeeze that happens just before the ventricles contract, so look for a small pressure bump on that low curve immediately before the big sharp rise to 20 kPa.
walkthrough:
**Identify the three pressure curves**

Think like this, big pumps make big pressures. The high curves peaking near $20 \text{ kPa}$ are ventricular pressure (dashed) and aortic pressure (solid).

The very low curve staying near $0$ to $2 \text{ kPa}$ (dotted) must be atrial pressure, because atria are thin walled and only push blood a short distance into the ventricles.

**Recall the order of the cardiac cycle**

The cycle starts with atrial systole, then ventricular systole, then diastole. So atrial contraction must appear as a small rise just before the ventricles fire.

Look at time about $0.8$ to $0.9 \text{ s}$. You see a small bump on the low dotted curve, followed immediately by the steep vertical rise of ventricular pressure.

**Match the arrows**

Arrow B points exactly to that small pre-ventricular bump on the atrial curve. That is the pressure rise caused by atrial systole pushing blood through the open atrioventricular valves.

Arrow A is the huge ventricular peak, C is after the bump when pressure falls, and D is the slow fall in aortic pressure.

options.A: Points to the peak near 20 kPa, which is ventricular systole when the thick ventricle wall contracts strongly, not the gentle atrial squeeze.
options.B: Points to the small rise in low atrial pressure just before ventricular pressure shoots up, which is exactly atrial systole filling the ventricles.
options.C: Points to the low pressure dip just as ventricular systole begins, when atrial pressure is falling during atrial diastole, not contracting.
options.D: Points to the gradually falling high pressure curve, which is aortic pressure dropping during ventricular diastole when blood flows out to the body.
